children.prompt: Find the general solution of $y'=-xy^2$ and the particular solution passing through $(2,0)$.

spec.sourceRegion: Right of the general-and-particular-solution working area
spec.description: Direction field with integer lattice segments from −4 to 4, both axes labelled at nonzero integers, arrowheads and no solution curve.
spec.mathematics: dy/dx=-xy^2; horizontal segments on both axes, positive slopes for x<0 and negative slopes for x>0.

answer.short: Nonconstant solutions: $y=\dfrac{2}{x^2+C}$. Constant solution: $y=0$. The particular solution through $(2,0)$ is $y=0$.
answer.worked:
For $y\ne0$,
$$\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{y^2}&=-x\,dx\\\int y^{-2}\,dy&=\int -x\,dx\\-\frac1y&=-\frac{x^2}{2}+C_1\\\frac2y&=x^2+C\\y&=\frac{2}{x^2+C}.\end{aligned}$$
Also, $y=0$ satisfies the original differential equation and was excluded when dividing by $y^2$. Thus the solutions include this constant solution as well as the nonconstant family, on intervals where its denominator is nonzero.

No member of the nonconstant family has $y=0$. The particular solution passing through $(2,0)$ is therefore $y=0$.

content.prompt: Use separation of variables to solve these DEs.

children.label: a
children.prompt: $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{2-y}{x}$

answer.worked: $$\begin{align*}\frac{1}{2-y}\,dy&=\frac{1}{x}\,dx\\\int\frac{1}{2-y}\,dy&=\int\frac{1}{x}\,dx\\-\ln|2-y|&=\ln|x|+C_1\\2-y&=\frac{C_2}{x}\\y&=2+\frac{C}{x}\end{align*}$$The constant solution $y=2$ is included by $C=0$. Here $x\ne0$.

children.label: b
children.prompt: $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{xy}{1+x^2}$

answer.worked: $$\begin{align*}\frac{1}{y}\,dy&=\frac{x}{1+x^2}\,dx\\\int\frac{1}{y}\,dy&=\int\frac{x}{1+x^2}\,dx\\\ln|y|&=\frac12\ln(1+x^2)+C_1\\y&=A\sqrt{1+x^2}\\y^2&=C(1+x^2)\end{align*}$$Here $A\in\mathbb R$ and $C=A^2\ge0$. The constant solution $y=0$ is included.

children.label: c
children.prompt: $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=-\dfrac{2y}{x}$

answer.worked: $$\begin{align*}\frac{1}{y}\,dy&=-\frac{2}{x}\,dx\\\int\frac{1}{y}\,dy&=-2\int\frac{1}{x}\,dx\\\ln|y|&=-2\ln|x|+C_1\\y&=\frac{C}{x^2}\end{align*}$$The constant solution $y=0$ is included by $C=0$. Here $x\ne0$.

children.label: d
children.prompt: $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=y\sin x$

answer.worked: $$\begin{align*}\frac{1}{y}\,dy&=\sin x\,dx\\\int\frac{1}{y}\,dy&=\int\sin x\,dx\\\ln|y|&=-\cos x+C_1\\y&=Ce^{-\cos x}\end{align*}$$The constant solution $y=0$ is included by $C=0$.

children.label: e
children.prompt: $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{3y}{x^2}$

answer.worked: $$\begin{align*}\frac{1}{y}\,dy&=\frac{3}{x^2}\,dx\\\int\frac{1}{y}\,dy&=\int3x^{-2}\,dx\\\ln|y|&=-\frac{3}{x}+C_1\\y&=Ce^{-3/x}\end{align*}$$The constant solution $y=0$ is included by $C=0$. Here $x\ne0$.

children.label: f
children.prompt: $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{y(1-x)}{x}$

answer.worked: $$\begin{align*}\frac{1}{y}\,dy&=\left(\frac{1}{x}-1\right)dx\\\int\frac{1}{y}\,dy&=\int\left(\frac{1}{x}-1\right)dx\\\ln|y|&=\ln|x|-x+C_1\\y&=Cxe^{-x}\end{align*}$$The constant solution $y=0$ is included by $C=0$. Here $x\ne0$.

children.label: a
children.prompt:
Explain why $y=0$, where $x\ne0$, is a solution of $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=-\dfrac{y^2}{x}$.

(Always look first for constant solutions.)

answer.short: For $y=0$, $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=0$ and $-\dfrac{y^2}{x}=0$, so both sides agree.
answer.worked:
If $y=0$, then $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=0$.

Substituting into the right-hand side gives
$$-\frac{0^2}{x}=0=\frac{dy}{dx}.$$
Thus $y=0$ is a solution for $x\ne0$.

children.label: b
children.prompt: Use the method of separable DEs to find the other solutions.

answer.worked:
For $y\ne0$,
$$\begin{align*}
\frac{1}{y^2}\,dy&=-\frac{1}{x}\,dx\\
\int\frac{1}{y^2}\,dy&=-\int\frac{1}{x}\,dx\\
-\frac{1}{y}&=-\ln|x|+C\\
\frac{1}{y}&=\ln|x|-C\\
y&=\frac{1}{\ln|x|+C}.
\end{align*}$$
The negative sign is absorbed into the arbitrary constant in the final line. The solution applies where $x\ne0$ and the denominator is nonzero.

content.prompt: Consider the DE $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{2y+4}{x}$.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Find the constant solution, substituting to show that it is a solution of the DE.

answer.worked:
For a constant solution, $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=0$, so
$$\begin{align*}
2y+4&=0\\
y&=-2.
\end{align*}$$
Substituting $y=-2$ into the right-hand side gives
$$\frac{2(-2)+4}{x}=0=\frac{dy}{dx},\qquad x\ne0.$$
Thus $y=-2$ is a solution.

children.label: b
children.prompt: Use separation of variables to find the other solutions of the DE.

answer.worked:
For $y\ne-2$,
$$\begin{align*}
\frac{1}{2y+4}\,dy&=\frac{1}{x}\,dx\\
\int\frac{1}{2y+4}\,dy&=\int\frac{1}{x}\,dx\\
\frac12\ln|2y+4|&=\ln|x|+C\\
\ln|2y+4|&=2\ln|x|+D\\
\ln|2y+4|&=\ln|x^2|+D\\
|2y+4|&=e^{\ln|x^2|+D}\\
|2y+4|&=e^D e^{\ln|x^2|}\\
2y+4&=\pm e^D x^2\\
y&=Ax^2-2.
\end{align*}$$
Here $D=2C$ and $A=\pm\dfrac{e^D}{2}\ne0$. These solutions apply for $x\ne0$.

children.label: c
children.prompt: How can the solutions in parts a and b be combined?

answer.short: Allow $A=0$: the full family is $y=Ax^2-2$ for all real $A$, with $x\ne0$.
answer.worked:
Setting $A=0$ in $y=Ax^2-2$ gives the constant solution $y=-2$. Thus the solutions combine as
$$y=Ax^2-2,\qquad A\in\mathbb R,\quad x\ne0.$$

content.prompt: Consider the DE $y'=-xy$.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Find the constant solution, substituting to show it is a solution of the DE.

answer.worked:
For a constant solution, $y'=0$, so $-xy=0$ for every $x$. Hence $y=0$.

Substituting $y=0$ into the right-hand side gives $$-x(0)=0=\frac{dy}{dx},$$ so $y=0$ is a solution.

children.label: b
children.prompt: Use separation of variables to find the other solutions of the DE.

answer.worked:
For $y\ne0$,
$$\begin{align*}
\frac{1}{y}\,dy&=-x\,dx\\
\int\frac{1}{y}\,dy&=\int-x\,dx\\
\ln|y|&=-\frac{x^2}{2}+C\\
|y|&=e^{-x^2/2+C}\\
y&=\pm e^C\cdot e^{-x^2/2}\\
y&=Ae^{-x^2/2}.
\end{align*}$$
Here $A=\pm e^C$, so $A\ne0$.

children.label: c
children.prompt: How can the solutions in parts a and b be combined?

answer.short: Allow $A=0$: the full solution is $y=Ae^{-x^2/2}$ for all real $A$.
answer.worked: Allow $A=0$ in $y=Ae^{-x^2/2}$. This gives the constant solution $y=0$, so the full solution is $$y=Ae^{-x^2/2},\qquad A\in\mathbb R.$$

children.label: a
children.prompt: Find all the constant solutions of $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=3x^2\cos^2 y$ in the interval $-2\pi\le y\le2\pi$.

answer.worked:
For a constant solution, $y'=0$, so $\cos^2 y=0$.
$$\begin{align*}
\cos y&=0\\
y&=\frac{\pi}{2}+k\pi,\qquad k\in\mathbb Z.
\end{align*}$$
In $-2\pi\le y\le2\pi$, the constant solutions are $$y=-\frac{3\pi}{2},\ -\frac{\pi}{2},\ \frac{\pi}{2},\ \frac{3\pi}{2}.$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: Find all the non-constant solutions.

answer.worked:
For $\cos y\ne0$,
$$\begin{align*}
\frac{1}{\cos^2 y}\,dy&=3x^2\,dx\\
\sec^2 y\,dy&=3x^2\,dx\\
\int\sec^2 y\,dy&=\int3x^2\,dx\\
\tan y&=x^3+C\\
y&=\tan^{-1}(x^3+C)+k\pi,\qquad k\in\mathbb Z.
\end{align*}$$
Here $C$ is any real constant; $k\pi$ includes every branch of the inverse tangent.

content.prompt: Consider the IVP $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{2y}{x-1}$ with $y(2)=1$.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Show that the constant solution of the DE is not a solution of the IVP.

answer.short: The constant solution is $y=0$, which gives $y(2)=0\ne1$.
answer.worked:
For a constant solution, $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=0$.
$$\begin{align*}0&=\frac{2y}{x-1}\\y&=0\end{align*}$$
This gives $y(2)=0\ne1$, so it is not a solution of the IVP.

children.label: b
children.prompt: Use separation of variables to find the general solution of the DE.

answer.short: $y=C(x-1)^2$, where $C$ is an arbitrary real constant and $x\ne1$.
answer.worked:
For $y\ne0$,
$$\begin{align*}\frac1y\,dy&=\frac2{x-1}\,dx\\\int\frac1y\,dy&=\int\frac2{x-1}\,dx\\\ln|y|&=2\ln|x-1|+C_1\\y&=C(x-1)^2\end{align*}$$
Allowing $C=0$ includes the constant solution. The DE requires $x\ne1$.

children.label: c
children.prompt: Hence solve the IVP.

answer.worked:
Substitute $x=2$, $y=1$:
$$\begin{align*}1&=C(2-1)^2\\C&=1\\y&=(x-1)^2\end{align*}$$
The interval containing the initial point is $x>1$.

content.prompt: Consider the IVP $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=(y-1)\tan x$ with $y\left(\dfrac\pi4\right)=3$.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Show that the constant solution of the DE is not a solution of the IVP.

answer.short: The constant solution is $y=1$, which gives $y\left(\dfrac\pi4\right)=1\ne3$.
answer.worked:
For a constant solution, $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=0$. Set the dependent-variable factor equal to zero:
$$\begin{align*}y-1&=0\\y&=1\end{align*}$$
This gives $y\left(\dfrac\pi4\right)=1\ne3$, so it is not a solution of the IVP.

children.label: b
children.prompt: Use separation of variables to find the general solution of the DE.

answer.short: $y=1+C\sec x$, where $C$ is an arbitrary real constant and $\cos x\ne0$.
answer.worked:
For $y\ne1$,
$$\begin{align*}\frac1{y-1}\,dy&=\tan x\,dx\\\int\frac1{y-1}\,dy&=\int\tan x\,dx\\\ln|y-1|&=-\ln|\cos x|+C_1\\\ln|y-1|&=\ln|\sec x|+C_1\\y-1&=A\sec x\\y&=1+C\sec x\end{align*}$$
Allowing $C=0$ includes the constant solution. The DE requires $\cos x\ne0$.

children.label: c
children.prompt: Hence solve the IVP.

answer.worked:
Substitute $x=\dfrac\pi4$, $y=3$:
$$\begin{align*}3-1&=C\sec\left(\frac\pi4\right)\\2&=C\sqrt2\\C&=\sqrt2\\y&=1+\sqrt2\sec x\end{align*}$$
The interval containing the initial point is $-\dfrac\pi2<x<\dfrac\pi2$.

children.label: a

children.label: b
children.prompt: Now suppose $(x,y)$ is on a curve where the tangent at any point passes through the origin. Write down a DE for this curve.

answer.worked:
The tangent passes through $(0,0)$ and $(x,y)$, so its gradient is $y/x$. Hence
$$\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{y}{x}.$$

children.label: c
children.prompt: Hence determine the general equation of this curve.

answer.worked:
For $y\ne0$, separate variables and integrate:
$$\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{y}&=\frac{dx}{x}\\\ln|y|&=\ln|x|+C\\\ln\left|\frac{y}{x}\right|&=C\\\frac{y}{x}&=A\\y&=Ax.\end{aligned}$$
The constant solution $y=0$ also satisfies the DE, so $A=0$ is included.

children.label: d
children.prompt: Which special case is a solution of the problem, but not of the DE?

answer.worked: The line $x=0$ is its own tangent and passes through the origin. It satisfies the geometric condition, but it is excluded from $dy/dx=y/x$: $y/x$ is undefined when $x=0$, and a vertical line has no finite gradient.

inlines.text: A wildlife conservancy models the lion population
The carrying capacity is 600 lions. The population satisfies the logistic equation
find the population equation and the population in 2026, to the nearest lion.

answer.short: $P(t)=\dfrac{600}{1+3e^{-t/6}}$, for $t\geq0$. In 2026, the population is approximately $285$ lions.
answer.worked:
Invert and use the supplied partial fractions:
$$\begin{aligned}\frac{dt}{dP}&=\frac{6}{P(1-P/600)}\\\frac{dt}{dP}&=\frac{3600}{P(600-P)}\\\frac{dt}{dP}&=6\left(\frac1P+\frac1{600-P}\right).\end{aligned}$$
Integrate and combine the logarithms:
$$\begin{aligned}t&=6\int\left(\frac1P+\frac1{600-P}\right)\,dP\\t&=6\bigl(\ln|P|-\ln|600-P|\bigr)+D\\\ln\left|\frac{P}{600-P}\right|&=\frac{t-D}{6}\\\frac{P}{600-P}&=Ae^{t/6}.\end{aligned}$$
Using $P(0)=150$:
$$\begin{aligned}\frac{150}{600-150}&=Ae^0\\A&=\frac13.\end{aligned}$$
Rearrange and write in standard form:
$$\begin{aligned}\frac{P}{600-P}&=\frac13e^{t/6}\\3P&=(600-P)e^{t/6}\\3P+Pe^{t/6}&=600e^{t/6}\\P(3+e^{t/6})&=600e^{t/6}\\P&=\frac{600e^{t/6}}{3+e^{t/6}}\\P&=\frac{600}{1+3e^{-t/6}},\qquad t\geq0.\end{aligned}$$
In 2026, $t=6$:
$$\begin{aligned}P(6)&=\frac{600}{1+3e^{-1}}\\P(6)&\approx285\text{ lions}.\end{aligned}$$

A seal colony satisfies $\dfrac{dP}{dt}=\dfrac14P\left(1-\dfrac{P}{800}\right)$, $P(0)=100$, $t$ in years.

$$\frac{800}{P(800-P)}=\frac1P+\frac1{800-P}.$$
Find $P(t)$, $P(8)$, and show that the long-term population is the carrying capacity. Give $P(8)$ to the nearest whole seal.

answer.short: $P(t)=\dfrac{800}{1+7e^{-t/4}}$; $P(8)\approx411$ seals. As $t\to\infty$, $P(t)\to800$ seals, the carrying capacity.
answer.worked:
$$\begin{aligned}
\frac{dt}{dP}&=\frac{3200}{P(800-P)}\\
\frac{dt}{dP}&=4\left(\frac1P+\frac1{800-P}\right)\\
t&=4\bigl(\ln|P|-\ln|800-P|\bigr)+D\\
\ln\left|\frac{P}{800-P}\right|&=\frac t4-\frac D4\\
\frac{P}{800-P}&=Ae^{t/4}.
\end{aligned}$$
Using $P(0)=100$,
$$\begin{aligned}
\frac{100}{700}&=Ae^0\\
A&=\frac17.
\end{aligned}$$
Hence
$$\begin{aligned}
\frac{P}{800-P}&=\frac17e^{t/4}\\
7P&=(800-P)e^{t/4}\\
P(7+e^{t/4})&=800e^{t/4}\\
P(t)&=\frac{800}{1+7e^{-t/4}}\\
P(8)&=\frac{800}{1+7e^{-2}}\\
P(8)&\approx411.
\end{aligned}$$

inlines.text: , explain why the rate of increase is greatest at half the carrying capacity.

answer.short: The rate is a downward-opening quadratic in $P$, with zeros at $0$ and $160\,000$. Its maximum is midway between them, at $P=80\,000$ cockroaches.
answer.worked:
The rate of increase is
$$\frac{dP}{dt}=\frac{3}{8000}P(160\,000-P).$$
As a function of $P$, this is a downward-opening parabola with roots $P=0$ and $P=160\,000$. These are the populations at which the rate of change is zero. By symmetry, its maximum occurs halfway between the roots:

Thus the rate of increase is greatest at half the carrying capacity.

content.prompt:
The height of a tree after $t$ years is given by $\dfrac{dQ}{dt}=0.03Q(45-Q)$.

The tree is $0.3$ m high when it is planted.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Evaluate $a$ and $b$ if $\dfrac{1}{Q(45-Q)}=\dfrac{a}{Q}+\dfrac{b}{45-Q}$.

answer.worked:
Multiply both sides by $Q(45-Q)$:
$$1=a(45-Q)+bQ.$$
Substitute $Q=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}1&=45a\\a&=\frac{1}{45}.\end{aligned}$$
Substitute $Q=45$:
$$\begin{aligned}1&=45b\\b&=\frac{1}{45}.\end{aligned}$$
Therefore,
$$\frac{1}{Q(45-Q)}=\frac{1}{45}\left(\frac{1}{Q}+\frac{1}{45-Q}\right).$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: Solve the differential equation to find the formula for the height of the tree.

answer.worked:
Separate variables:
$$\frac{1}{Q(45-Q)}\,dQ=0.03\,dt.$$
Using partial fractions from (a):
$$\frac{1}{45}\left(\frac{1}{Q}+\frac{1}{45-Q}\right)\,dQ=0.03\,dt.$$
Integrate both sides and combine the logarithms:
$$\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{45}\left(\ln|Q|-\ln|45-Q|\right)&=0.03t+C_1\\\ln\left|\frac{Q}{45-Q}\right|&=1.35t+C_2\\\frac{Q}{45-Q}&=Ae^{1.35t}.\end{aligned}$$
Substitute $Q=0.3$ when $t=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}\frac{0.3}{44.7}&=A\\A&=\frac{1}{149}.\end{aligned}$$
Hence,
$$\begin{aligned}\frac{Q}{45-Q}&=\frac{1}{149}e^{1.35t}\\149Q&=(45-Q)e^{1.35t}\\149Q+Qe^{1.35t}&=45e^{1.35t}\\Q(149+e^{1.35t})&=45e^{1.35t}\\Q&=\frac{45e^{1.35t}}{149+e^{1.35t}}.\end{aligned}$$
Divide the numerator and denominator by $e^{1.35t}$:
$$Q=\frac{45}{1+149e^{-1.35t}}\text{ metres},\qquad t\geq0.$$

content.prompt:
Biologists model a fish population $y$ (in hundreds) using:
$$\frac{dy}{dt}=-2+\frac{1}{24}y(16-y)$$
where $t$ is years after the next harvest. The December count indicates 500 fish. Assume the next harvest removes 200 fish immediately after this count.

children.label: a
children.prompt: What is the significance of the $-2$ in the equation?

answer.short: Fish are harvested at a rate of 200 fish per year.
answer.worked: Since $y$ is measured in hundreds of fish and $t$ in years, the term $-2$ represents removal of 200 fish per year.

children.label: b
children.prompt: Show the DE can be rewritten as $\dfrac{dy}{dt}=-\dfrac{1}{24}(y-4)(y-12)$, and write down the initial condition assuming the harvest goes ahead.

answer.short: $\dfrac{dy}{dt}=-\dfrac{1}{24}(y-4)(y-12)$. Assuming the next harvest removes 200 fish immediately, $y(0)=3$.
answer.worked:
$$\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dt}&=-2+\frac{1}{24}y(16-y)\\\frac{dy}{dt}&=\frac{1}{24}\bigl(-48+y(16-y)\bigr)\\\frac{dy}{dt}&=-\frac{1}{24}(y^2-16y+48)\\\frac{dy}{dt}&=-\frac{1}{24}(y-4)(y-12).\end{aligned}$$
The supplied solution assumes an immediate harvest of 200 fish. Under this assumption, $y(0)=\dfrac{500-200}{100}=3$.

children.label: c
children.prompt: Show that $\dfrac{24}{(y-4)(y-12)}=\dfrac{3}{y-12}-\dfrac{3}{y-4}$.

children.label: d
children.prompt: Hence solve the IVP in part b.

answer.worked:
Using the supplied solution's assumption $y(0)=3$:
$$\begin{aligned}\frac{dt}{dy}&=-\frac{24}{(y-4)(y-12)}\\\frac{dt}{dy}&=-\left(\frac{3}{y-12}-\frac{3}{y-4}\right).\end{aligned}$$
Integrating gives
$$\begin{aligned}-t+D&=3\ln|y-12|-3\ln|y-4|\\3\ln\left|\frac{y-12}{y-4}\right|&=-t+D\\\ln\left|\frac{y-12}{y-4}\right|&=-\frac{t}{3}+D_1\\\frac{y-12}{y-4}&=Ae^{-t/3}.\end{aligned}$$
Apply $y(0)=3$:
$$\begin{aligned}\frac{3-12}{3-4}&=Ae^0\\A&=9.\end{aligned}$$
Therefore
$$\begin{aligned}\frac{y-12}{y-4}&=9e^{-t/3}\\y-12&=9e^{-t/3}(y-4)\\y(1-9e^{-t/3})&=12-36e^{-t/3}\\y&=\frac{12-36e^{-t/3}}{1-9e^{-t/3}}\\y&=\frac{12(1-3e^{-t/3})}{1-9e^{-t/3}}.\end{aligned}$$

children.label: e
children.prompt: According to this model, when will the fish die out? Give an exact answer and an approximation to the nearest tenth of a year.

answer.short: Assuming $y(0)=3$, $3\ln3\approx3.3$ years after the next harvest.
answer.worked:
Using the solution with $y(0)=3$, extinction occurs when $y=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}1-3e^{-t/3}&=0\\e^{-t/3}&=\frac13\\-\frac{t}{3}&=-\ln3\\t&=3\ln3\\t&\approx3.3\text{ years}.\end{aligned}$$
The denominator is $1-9\left(\frac13\right)=-2\ne0$, so this gives zero population. The fish die out about 3.3 years after the next harvest.

answer.short: $\displaystyle N=\frac{1000}{1+Be^{-1000kt}}$, where $B$ is an arbitrary constant. Also $N=0$ is a constant solution.
answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}\frac{dN}{N(1000-N)}&=k\,dt\\\frac1{1000}\left(\frac1N+\frac1{1000-N}\right)dN&=k\,dt.\end{align*}$$
Integrate:
$$\begin{align*}\frac1{1000}\bigl(\ln|N|-\ln|1000-N|\bigr)&=kt+C\\\ln\left|\frac{N}{1000-N}\right|&=1000kt+C_1\\\frac{N}{1000-N}&=Ae^{1000kt}.\end{align*}$$
Rearranging:
$$\begin{align*}N&=1000Ae^{1000kt}-NAe^{1000kt}\\N(1+Ae^{1000kt})&=1000Ae^{1000kt}\\N&=\frac{1000}{1+Be^{-1000kt}},\end{align*}$$
where $B=1/A$. The constant solutions are $N=0$ and $N=1000$; the latter is included by taking $B=0$.

children.label: c
children.prompt: Determine the arbitrary constant using $N(0)=40$, then simplify.

children.label: d
children.prompt: Given the population after 1 year was 80, find $k$ correct to four significant figures.

children.label: e
children.prompt: What will the population be after 5 years, to the nearest whole number?

$$\begin{align*}N(5)&=\frac{1000}{1+24e^{-5000k}}\\&=\frac{1000}{1+24\left(\frac{11.5}{24}\right)^5}\\&\approx623.\end{align*}$$
The population will be approximately 623 animals.

content.prompt:
Pierre-François Verhulst (1838) modelled US population growth using:
$$\dot N=kN(P-N),$$
for some positive constant $k$, where $N$ is population in millions and $t$ is years after 1850.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Show that $\dfrac{P}{N(P-N)}=\dfrac1N+\dfrac1{P-N}$.

children.label: b
children.prompt: Use part a to find the general solution.

answer.short: $N=\dfrac{P}{1+Be^{-kPt}}$, where $B$ is an arbitrary constant. Also $N=0$ is a constant solution.
answer.worked:
For nonconstant solutions,
$$\begin{align*}\frac{dt}{dN}&=\frac{1}{kN(P-N)}\\&=\frac1{kP}\left(\frac1N+\frac1{P-N}\right),\\t&=\frac1{kP}\bigl(\ln|N|-\ln|P-N|\bigr)+D,\\\ln\left|\frac{N}{P-N}\right|&=kPt+C,\\\frac{N}{P-N}&=Ae^{kPt},\\N&=Ae^{kPt}(P-N),\\N(1+Ae^{kPt})&=PAe^{kPt},\\N&=\frac{PAe^{kPt}}{1+Ae^{kPt}}\\&=\frac{P}{1+Be^{-kPt}},\qquad B=\frac1A.\end{align*}$$
The constant solutions are $N=0$ and $N=P$; the latter is included by $B=0$.

children.label: c
children.prompt: $P=187.5$ and $N(0)=23.2$ (millions). Determine the arbitrary constant and simplify.

children.label: d
children.prompt: The estimate $k=1.6\times10^{-4}$ predicted 59.8 million in 1890. The actual population was 63.0 million. Calculate a new value for $k$, giving your answer to 4 significant figures.

children.label: e
children.prompt: Using the revised $k$, compare the predicted population for 1930 with the actual figure of 123.2 million. Give the predicted population to 1 decimal place.

answer.short: 120.9 million, approximately 2.3 million below the actual population. The model slightly underestimates.
answer.worked:
For 1930, $t=80$. Using the unrounded value of $k$ from part d,
$$\begin{align*}N(80)&=\frac{23.2\times187.5}{23.2+164.3e^{-187.5k(80)}}\\&\approx120.9\text{ million}.\end{align*}$$
The prediction is approximately $123.2-120.9=2.3$ million below the actual population, so the model is reasonably close but slightly underestimates.

children.label: f
children.prompt: The US population in 2018 was approximately 327 million. Comment on this value.

answer.short: 327 million exceeds the assumed carrying capacity of 187.5 million, so the model's carrying capacity was too low.
answer.worked: Since the initial population is below $P=187.5$ million, this model predicts a population that approaches 187.5 million from below. The actual 327 million is far greater, showing that the assumed carrying capacity was too low and the model is unsuitable for this long-term prediction.

content.prompt:
A lake is stocked with 600 fish; the carrying capacity is 12 000. The population $N$ satisfies
$$\frac{dN}{dt}=kN(12\,000-N),$$
with $t$ in years. You may use
$$\frac{12\,000}{N(12\,000-N)}=\frac1N+\frac1{12\,000-N}.$$

answer.worked:
The alternate notation gives the scaling
$$\begin{align*}\frac{dt}{dN}&=\frac1{kN(12\,000-N)}\\\frac{dt}{dN}&=\frac1{12\,000k}\left(\frac1N+\frac1{12\,000-N}\right).
\end{align*}$$
Integrating gives
$$\begin{align*}t&=\frac1{12\,000k}\left(\ln|N|-\ln|12\,000-N|\right)+D\\\ln\left|\frac{N}{12\,000-N}\right|&=12\,000kt+D_1\\\frac{N}{12\,000-N}&=Ae^{12\,000kt}.
\end{align*}$$
Thus the exponent is $12\,000kt$. Using $N(0)=600$,
$$\begin{align*}A&=\frac{600}{11\,400}\\A&=\frac1{19}.
\end{align*}$$
Hence
$$\begin{align*}19N&=(12\,000-N)e^{12\,000kt}\\19N+Ne^{12\,000kt}&=12\,000e^{12\,000kt}\\N(19+e^{12\,000kt})&=12\,000e^{12\,000kt}\\N&=\frac{12\,000e^{12\,000kt}}{19+e^{12\,000kt}}\\N&=\frac{12\,000}{1+19e^{-12\,000kt}}.
\end{align*}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: The population doubled during the first year. Find $k$.

children.label: c
children.prompt: Find, to the nearest month, how long it takes the population to reach 9000.

answer.worked:
Set $N=9000$:
$$\begin{align*}1+19e^{-12\,000kt}&=\frac{12\,000}{9000}=\frac43\\e^{-12\,000kt}&=\frac1{57}\\12\,000kt&=\ln57.
\end{align*}$$
Since $12\,000k=\ln\dfrac{19}{9}$,
$$\begin{align*}t&=\frac{\ln57}{\ln(19/9)}\\t&\approx5.411\text{ years}\\12t&\approx65\text{ months}.
\end{align*}$$
The population reaches 9000 after 65 months, to the nearest month.

content.prompt:
A town’s population $P$ satisfies
$$\frac{dP}{dt}=0.04P\left(\frac{C-P}{C}\right),$$
where $t$ is years after 2005 and $C$ is the carrying capacity.

In 2005 the population was $40\,000$; in 2025 it was $70\,000$.

Use $\dfrac{C}{P(C-P)}=\dfrac{1}{P}+\dfrac{1}{C-P}$ to find the carrying capacity, to the nearest thousand.

answer.worked:
Separating variables and using the supplied identity,
$$\begin{align*}
\frac{C}{P(C-P)}\,dP&=0.04\,dt\\
\int\left(\frac1P+\frac1{C-P}\right)\,dP&=\int0.04\,dt\\
\ln P-\ln(C-P)&=0.04t+k\\
\ln\left(\frac{P}{C-P}\right)&=0.04t+k\\
\frac{P}{C-P}&=Ae^{0.04t}.
\end{align*}$$
The two data points give
$$\begin{align*}
\frac{40\,000}{C-40\,000}&=A\\
\frac{70\,000}{C-70\,000}&=Ae^{0.8}.
\end{align*}$$
Dividing eliminates $A$:
$$\begin{align*}
\frac{70\,000(C-40\,000)}{40\,000(C-70\,000)}&=e^{0.8}\\
\frac{7(C-40\,000)}{4(C-70\,000)}&=e^{0.8}\\
7(C-40\,000)&=4e^{0.8}(C-70\,000)\\
(4e^{0.8}-7)C&=280\,000(e^{0.8}-1)\\
C&=\frac{280\,000(e^{0.8}-1)}{4e^{0.8}-7}.
\end{align*}$$
The carrying capacity is therefore $180\,000$ people, to the nearest thousand.

answer.worked:
Separate variables and use the supplied partial fractions:
$$\begin{aligned}
\int\left(\frac1P+\frac1{C-P}\right)\,dP&=\int0.1\,dt\\
\ln|P|-\ln|C-P|&=0.1t+k\\
\frac{P}{C-P}&=Ae^{0.1t}.
\end{aligned}$$
At $t=0$, $P=200\,000$; at $t=20$, $P=500\,000$:
$$\begin{aligned}
\frac{200\,000}{C-200\,000}&=A\\
\frac{500\,000}{C-500\,000}&=Ae^2.
\end{aligned}$$
Divide the second equation by the first:
$$\begin{aligned}
\frac{5(C-200\,000)}{2(C-500\,000)}&=e^2\\
5(C-200\,000)&=2e^2(C-500\,000)\\
(2e^2-5)C&=1\,000\,000(e^2-1)\\
C&=\frac{1\,000\,000(e^2-1)}{2e^2-5}\\
C&\approx653\,000.
\end{aligned}$$
The carrying capacity is $653\,000$ deer, to the nearest thousand.

content.prompt:
A kangaroo population is modelled by
$$K=\frac{12\,000}{4+e^{-t/4}}$$
where $t$ is years from today.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Show that $K$ satisfies $\dfrac{dK}{dt}=\dfrac14K\left(1-\dfrac{K}{3000}\right)$.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}K&=12\,000(4+e^{-t/4})^{-1}\\\frac{dK}{dt}&=12\,000(-1)(4+e^{-t/4})^{-2}\left(-\frac14e^{-t/4}\right)\\&=\frac{3000e^{-t/4}}{(4+e^{-t/4})^2}.\end{align*}$$
Check by substitution:
$$\begin{align*}\mathrm{RHS}&=\frac14\left(\frac{12\,000}{4+e^{-t/4}}\right)\left(1-\frac{\frac{12\,000}{4+e^{-t/4}}}{3000}\right)\\&=\frac14\left(\frac{12\,000}{4+e^{-t/4}}\right)\left(1-\frac4{4+e^{-t/4}}\right)\\&=\frac14\left(\frac{12\,000}{4+e^{-t/4}}\right)\left(\frac{4+e^{-t/4}-4}{4+e^{-t/4}}\right)\\&=\frac14\left(\frac{12\,000}{4+e^{-t/4}}\right)\left(\frac{e^{-t/4}}{4+e^{-t/4}}\right)\\&=\frac{3000e^{-t/4}}{(4+e^{-t/4})^2}\\&=\mathrm{LHS}.\end{align*}$$
Thus $K$ satisfies the differential equation.

children.label: b
children.prompt: What is the population today?

answer.worked:
Today, $t=0$:
$$\begin{align*}K(0)&=\frac{12\,000}{4+1}\\&=2400.\end{align*}$$
The population today is 2400 kangaroos.

children.label: c
children.prompt: What eventual population does the model predict?

answer.worked:
As $t\to\infty$, $e^{-t/4}\to0$, so
$$K\to\frac{12\,000}{4}=3000.$$
The model predicts an eventual population of 3000 kangaroos.

children.label: d
children.prompt: What is the annual percentage growth rate today?

answer.worked:
At $t=0$, $K=2400$:
$$\begin{align*}\left.\frac{dK}{dt}\right|_{t=0}&=\frac14(2400)\left(1-\frac{2400}{3000}\right)\\&=120\text{ kangaroos per year}.\end{align*}$$
$$\text{Percentage growth rate}=\frac{120}{2400}\times100\%=5\%\text{ per year}.$$

children.prompt: Find the initial population and the limiting population.

answer.short: Initial population: 20 yabbies. Limiting population: 300 yabbies.
answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}y(0)&=\frac{300}{1+14}\\&=20.\end{align*}$$
As $t\to\infty$, $e^{-0.4t}\to0$, so $y\to300$.
The population starts at 20 yabbies and approaches a limit of 300 yabbies.

children.label: b
children.prompt: Find the population when it is growing fastest.

answer.worked:
For a logistic model, the growth rate is greatest at half the limiting population.
$$\begin{align*}y&=\frac{300}{2}\\&=150.\end{align*}$$
The population is growing fastest at 150 yabbies.

children.label: c
children.prompt: Find the exact time at which it is growing fastest.

answer.worked:
Set $y=150$:
$$\begin{align*}150&=\frac{300}{1+14e^{-0.4t}}\\1+14e^{-0.4t}&=2\\e^{-0.4t}&=\frac{1}{14}\\-0.4t&=\ln\frac{1}{14}\\t&=\frac{5}{2}\ln14\text{ months}.\end{align*}$$
This is approximately $6.6$ months after release.

content.prompt:
The temperature of an object changes at a rate proportional to the difference between its temperature $T$ and the ambient temperature $A$.
A cup of coffee cools from $90^\circ\mathrm{C}$ to $70^\circ\mathrm{C}$ in 5 minutes in a room at $20^\circ\mathrm{C}$.
Form and solve the differential equation for $T$ as a function of time $t$, measured in minutes.

answer.short: $\dfrac{dT}{dt}=k(T-20)$, where $k=\dfrac15\ln\dfrac57$; $T=20+70e^{\frac15\ln(5/7)t}$, with $T$ in $^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and $t$ in minutes.
answer.worked:
$$\begin{aligned}\frac{dT}{dt}&=k(T-20),\quad k<0\\\frac{dT}{T-20}&=k\,dt\\\ln|T-20|&=kt+C\\T-20&=Be^{kt}\\T&=20+Be^{kt}.\end{aligned}$$
Using $T(0)=90$ gives $B=70$.
$$\begin{aligned}70&=20+70e^{5k}\\\frac57&=e^{5k}\\k&=\frac15\ln\frac57\\T&=20+70e^{\frac15\ln(5/7)t}.\end{aligned}$$
Here $T$ is in $^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and $t$ is in minutes.

content.prompt:
Solve the differential equation $\frac{dy}{dx}=3x^2e^{-y}$, given $y(0)=1$.
Express your answer with $y$ as the subject.

answer.worked:
Separate the variables.
$$\begin{align*}
\frac{dy}{dx} &= 3x^2e^{-y} \\
e^y\frac{dy}{dx} &= 3x^2 \\
e^y\,dy &= 3x^2\,dx
\end{align*}$$
Integrate both sides.
$$\begin{align*}
\int e^y\,dy &= \int 3x^2\,dx \\
e^y &= x^3+C
\end{align*}$$
Use $y(0)=1$.
$$\begin{align*}
e^1 &= 0^3+C \\
C &= e
\end{align*}$$
Therefore:
$$\begin{align*}
e^y &= x^3+e \\
y &= \ln(x^3+e)
\end{align*}$$

content.prompt:
A baseball player’s throwing speed has been increasing exponentially as part of an intense training program.
Over the last 6 weeks, his throwing speed has increased by 8%.
Assuming the same exponential growth continues, how long will it take for his throwing speed to increase by 30%?
Give your answer to 2 decimal places.
Use the exponential growth model $S(t)=S_0e^{kt}$, where $S_0$ is the initial throwing speed, $t$ is the time in weeks and $k$ is a constant.

answer.worked:
After 6 weeks:
$$\begin{align*}1.08S_0&=S_0e^{6k}\\k&=\frac{\ln1.08}{6}\end{align*}$$
For a $30\%$ increase:
$$\begin{align*}1.30&=e^{kt}\\t&=\frac{\ln1.30}{k}=\frac{6\ln1.30}{\ln1.08}\approx20.45\end{align*}$$
It will take $20.45$ weeks.

content.prompt:
The population, $P$, of kangaroos in a reservation is modelled by the logistic equation
$$\frac{dP}{dt}=2P\left(5-\frac{P}{10\,000}\right)$$

It is estimated that initially the population of the kangaroos is $15\%$ of the carrying capacity of the reservation.

children.label: i
children.prompt: What is the initial population of the kangaroos?

answer.worked:
The carrying capacity is where $\frac{dP}{dt}=0$ for $P>0$:
$$5-\frac P{10\,000}=0\quad\Rightarrow\quad P=50\,000$$
Initial population $=0.15\times50\,000=7500$.

children.label: ii
children.prompt: What is the population of the kangaroos when the rate of increase is a maximum?

answer.worked:
The rate $\frac{dP}{dt}$ is a quadratic in $P$ with zeros at $P=0$ and $P=50\,000$, so it is greatest halfway between them:
$$P=\frac{50\,000}2=25\,000$$

answer.worked:

$$\frac13\left(1-\frac K{3000}\right)K=\frac13\cdot\frac{3e^{-t/3}}u\cdot\frac{21000}u=\frac{21000e^{-t/3}}{u^2}$$
The two sides are equal.

content.prompt:
A quantity of a radioactive material decays according to the differential equation $\dfrac{dM}{dt}=-kM$, where $M$ is the mass of the material in kg, $t$ is the time in years and $k$ is constant.

The initial amount of the material is $20$ kg.

children.label: i

children.label: ii
children.prompt:
The half-life of the material is $300$ years.

Find the quantity of the material that is left after $500$ years.

Give your answer correct to one decimal place.

answer.worked:
At the half-life, $M=10$ when $t=300$:
$$\begin{align*}10&=20e^{-300k}\\\frac12&=e^{-300k}\\\ln\left(\frac12\right)&=-300k\\k&=\frac{\ln2}{300}\end{align*}$$
After $500$ years:
$$\begin{align*}M&=20e^{-500k}\\&=20e^{-\frac{500\ln2}{300}}\\&\approx6.2996\end{align*}$$
There is $6.3$ kg of material left after $500$ years.

children.label: iii
children.prompt: Draw a neat sketch of the Mass function against time, showing the information found in part ii.

answer.short: Exponential decay curve through $(0,20)$, $(300,10)$ and $(500,6.3)$, approaching the $t$-axis.
answer.worked: The sketch is the decaying exponential $M=20e^{-\frac{\ln2}{300}t}$, passing through $(0,20)$, $(300,10)$ and $(500,6.3)$.

content.prompt:
Find the particular solution to the differential equation
$$(x-2)\frac{dy}{dx}=xy$$
that passes through the point $(0, 1)$.

answer.worked:
Separate the variables:
$$\begin{align*}
(x-2)\frac{dy}{dx} &= xy \\
\frac{1}{y} \, dy &= \frac{x}{x-2} \, dx
\end{align*}$$
Integrate both sides. To integrate the right-hand side, manipulate the numerator:
$$\begin{align*}
\int \frac{1}{y} \, dy &= \int \frac{x-2+2}{x-2} \, dx \\
\int \frac{1}{y} \, dy &= \int \left( 1 + \frac{2}{x-2} \right) \, dx \\
\ln|y| &= x + 2\ln|x-2| + C \\
\ln|y| &= x + \ln(|x-2|^2) + C \\
\ln|y| - \ln((x-2)^2) &= x + C \\
\ln\left(\frac{|y|}{(x-2)^2}\right) &= x + C \\
\frac{|y|}{(x-2)^2} &= e^{x+C} \\
|y| &= e^C e^x (x-2)^2 \\
y &= A e^x (x-2)^2 \quad (\text{where } A = \pm e^C)
\end{align*}$$
Use the initial condition that the curve passes through $(0, 1)$:
$$\begin{align*}
1 &= A e^0 (0-2)^2 \\
1 &= A(1)(-2)^2 \\
1 &= 4A \\
A &= \frac{1}{4}
\end{align*}$$
Substitute $A = \frac{1}{4}$ back into the general solution:
$$\begin{align*}
y &= \frac{1}{4} e^x (x-2)^2
\end{align*}$$

content.prompt:
A salad, which is initially at a temperature of $25^\circ\text{C}$, is placed in a refrigerator that has a constant temperature of $3^\circ\text{C}$.
The cooling rate of the salad is proportional to the difference between the temperature of the refrigerator and the temperature, $T$, of the salad.
That is, $T$ satisfies the equation
$$\frac{dT}{dt} = -k(T - 3),$$
where $t$ is the number of minutes after the salad is placed in the refrigerator.
$\textbf{(i)}$ Show that $T = 3 + Ae^{-kt}$ satisfies this equation.

$\textbf{(ii)}$ The temperature of the salad is $11^\circ\text{C}$ after $10$ minutes.
Find the temperature of the salad after $15$ minutes.

answer.worked:
$\textbf{(i)}$
$$\begin{align*}
T &= 3 + Ae^{-kt} \\
\frac{dT}{dt} &= -kAe^{-kt} \\
&= -k(T - 3)
\end{align*}$$
Hence $T = 3 + Ae^{-kt}$ satisfies the differential equation.

$\textbf{(ii)}$
$$\begin{align*}
\text{At } t = 0, T = 25: \\
25 &= 3 + Ae^0 \\
A &= 22 \\
& \quad \\
\text{At } t = 10, T = 11: \\
11 &= 3 + 22e^{-10k} \\
8 &= 22e^{-10k} \\
e^{-10k} &= \frac{4}{11} \\
-10k &= \ln\left(\frac{4}{11}\right) \\
k &= -\frac{1}{10} \ln\left(\frac{4}{11}\right) \approx 0.10116 \\
& \quad \\
\text{At } t = 15: \\
T &= 3 + 22e^{-15k} \\
&= 3 + 22e^{-15\left(-\frac{1}{10} \ln\left(\frac{4}{11}\right)\right)} \\
&= 3 + 22\left(\frac{4}{11}\right)^{\frac{3}{2}} \\
&\approx 7.8^\circ\text{C}
\end{align*}$$

content.prompt:
The area $A\text{ cm}^2$ is occupied by a bacterial colony.
The colony has its growth modelled by the logistic equation
$$\frac{dA}{dt}=\frac{1}{25}A(50-A),$$
where $t\geq0$ and $t$ is measured in days.
At time $t=0$, the area occupied by the bacteria colony is $\frac{1}{2}\text{ cm}^2$.

children.label: a
children.prompt:
Show that
$$\frac{1}{A(50-A)}=\frac{1}{50}\left(\frac{1}{A}+\frac{1}{50-A}\right).$$

children.label: b
children.prompt:
Using the result from part a, solve the logistic equation and hence show that
$$A=\frac{50}{1+99e^{-2t}}.$$

answer.worked:
Separate variables:
$$\begin{align*}
\frac{dA}{dt} &= \frac{1}{25}A(50-A) \\
\frac{25}{A(50-A)}\,dA &= dt
\end{align*}$$
Using the result from part a:
$$\begin{align*}
\int \frac{25}{A(50-A)}\,dA &= \int 1\,dt \\
\int \frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{1}{A}+\frac{1}{50-A}\right)\,dA &= \int 1\,dt \\
\frac{1}{2}(\ln A-\ln(50-A)) &= t+C \\
\ln\left(\frac{A}{50-A}\right) &= 2t+C_1 \\
\frac{A}{50-A} &= Ce^{2t}
\end{align*}$$
At $t=0$, $A=\frac{1}{2}$:
$$\begin{align*}
C &= \frac{\frac{1}{2}}{50-\frac{1}{2}} \\
&= \frac{\frac{1}{2}}{\frac{99}{2}} \\
&= \frac{1}{99}
\end{align*}$$
So:
$$\begin{align*}
\frac{A}{50-A} &= \frac{e^{2t}}{99} \\
99Ae^{-2t} &= 50-A \\
A(1+99e^{-2t}) &= 50 \\
A &= \frac{50}{1+99e^{-2t}}
\end{align*}$$

children.label: c
children.prompt: According to this model, what is the limiting area of the bacteria colony?

answer.worked:
As $t\to\infty$, $e^{-2t}\to0$. Therefore:
$$\begin{align*}
A &\to \frac{50}{1+0} \\
&= 50
\end{align*}$$
The limiting area is $50\text{ cm}^2$.

children.label: d
children.prompt: Find the exact time when the rate of change in the area occupied by the bacterial colony is at its maximum.

answer.worked:
The rate of change is:
$$\begin{align*}
\frac{dA}{dt} &= \frac{1}{25}A(50-A)
\end{align*}$$
This is a quadratic in $A$ with maximum at $A=25$. Hence:
$$\begin{align*}
25 &= \frac{50}{1+99e^{-2t}} \\
25(1+99e^{-2t}) &= 50 \\
1+99e^{-2t} &= 2 \\
99e^{-2t} &= 1 \\
e^{2t} &= 99 \\
t &= \frac{1}{2}\ln99
\end{align*}$$
The exact time is $\frac{1}{2}\ln99$ days.

A scientist is studying a population of mice on an island.

answer.worked:

content.prompt:
A possum population on an island has maximum capacity $1000$.
Let $P$ be the population at time $t$ years, modelled by $\frac{dP}{dt}=kP(1000-P)$, where $k>0$.
It is given that $\frac1{P(1000-P)}=\frac1{1000P}+\frac1{1000(1000-P)}$.
If the population was $100$ possums two years ago and $400$ possums one year ago, estimate the current possum population.

answer.worked:
Let $t=0$ be two years ago, so $P(0)=100$, $P(1)=400$, and the current population is $P(2)$.
$$\begin{align*}\frac1{1000}\left(\frac1P+\frac1{1000-P}\right)dP&=k\,dt\\\ln P-\ln(1000-P)&=1000kt+C\\\frac P{1000-P}&=Ae^{1000kt}\end{align*}$$
Using $P(0)=100$: $A=\frac19$. Using $P(1)=400$:
$$\frac{400}{600}=\frac19e^{1000k}\quad\Rightarrow\quad e^{1000k}=6$$
So $\frac P{1000-P}=\frac19\cdot6^t$. At $t=2$: $\frac P{1000-P}=4$, so $P=800$.
The current population is about $800$ possums.

content.prompt:
The spread of a flu through a population is modelled by the equation
$$S=\frac{2000}{1+199e^{-0.4t}}$$
where $S$ is the total number of people infected after $t$ days.

children.label: i
children.prompt:
Show that the given equation for $S$ satisfies the differential equation
$$\frac{dS}{dt}=\frac{S}{5}\left(2-\frac{S}{1000}\right)$$

children.label: ii
children.prompt:
The slope field of $\dfrac{dS}{dt}=\dfrac{S}{5}\left(2-\dfrac{S}{1000}\right)$ is shown.

The three regions $A$, $B$ and $C$ in which a solution curve can be found, have been labelled and shaded correspondingly.

State which region the given solution curve $S$ can exist in and justify your answer with reference to its constant solutions.

answer.short: Region $B$, since $S(0)=10$ lies between the constant solutions $S=0$ and $S=2000$.
answer.worked:
The constant solutions occur when $\dfrac{dS}{dt}=0$.
$$\begin{align*}\frac{S}{5}\left(2-\frac{S}{1000}\right)&=0\\S&=0\quad\text{or}\quad S=2000\end{align*}$$
At $t=0$:
$$\begin{align*}S(0)&=\frac{2000}{1+199e^0}\\&=\frac{2000}{200}\\&=10\end{align*}$$
Since $S(0)=10$ lies between the constant solutions $S=0$ and $S=2000$, the given solution curve exists in region $B$.

The axes are drawn on top of the shading and slope segments so the S-axis remains fully visible.

children.label: iii
children.prompt:
Using this model, find on which day the rate of increase reaches a maximum.

Give your answer correct to the nearest day.

answer.short: $t\approx13$ days ($t\approx13.23$), so the maximum rate occurs during the $14$th day.
answer.worked:
The rate of increase is
$$\frac{dS}{dt}=\frac{S}{5}\left(2-\frac{S}{1000}\right).$$
This is a downward-opening quadratic in $S$ with roots $S=0$ and $S=2000$, so its maximum occurs halfway between the roots.
$$\begin{align*}S&=\frac{0+2000}{2}\\&=1000\end{align*}$$
Now solve for $t$ when $S=1000$:
$$\begin{align*}1000&=\frac{2000}{1+199e^{-0.4t}}\\1+199e^{-0.4t}&=2\\e^{-0.4t}&=\frac{1}{199}\\-0.4t&=\ln\left(\frac{1}{199}\right)\\t&=-\frac{1}{0.4}\ln\left(\frac{1}{199}\right)\\&\approx13.23\end{align*}$$
Thus $t\approx13$ days to the nearest day, and this falls during the $14$th day.

content.prompt:
Some yabbies are introduced into a small dam.
The size of the population, $y$, of yabbies can be modelled by the function
$$y = \frac{200}{1+19e^{-0.5t}}$$
where $t$ is the time in months after the yabbies are introduced into the dam.
$\textbf{(i)}$ Show that the rate of growth of the size of the population is
$$\frac{1900e^{-0.5t}}{(1+19e^{-0.5t})^2}$$

$\textbf{(ii)}$ Find the range of the function $y$, justifying your answer.

$\textbf{(iii)}$ Show that the rate of growth of the size of the population can be rewritten as
$$\frac{y}{400}(200-y)$$

$\textbf{(iv)}$ Hence, find the size of the population when it is growing at its fastest rate.

answer.worked:
$\textbf{(i)}$
Let $y = 200(1+19e^{-0.5t})^{-1}$. Use the chain rule:
$$\begin{align*}
\frac{dy}{dt} &= -200(1+19e^{-0.5t})^{-2} \times \frac{d}{dt}(1+19e^{-0.5t}) \\
&= -200(1+19e^{-0.5t})^{-2} \times (19 \times -0.5e^{-0.5t}) \\
&= \frac{-200 \times -9.5e^{-0.5t}}{(1+19e^{-0.5t})^2} \\
&= \frac{1900e^{-0.5t}}{(1+19e^{-0.5t})^2}
\end{align*}$$

$\textbf{(ii)}$
Find $y$ at $t = 0$:
$$\begin{align*}
y(0) &= \frac{200}{1 + 19e^0} \\
&= \frac{200}{1 + 19} = \frac{200}{20} = 10
\end{align*}$$
Find the limit of $y$ as $t \to \infty$:
As $t \to \infty$, $e^{-0.5t} \to 0$, so:
$$\begin{align*}
\lim_{t \to \infty} y &= \frac{200}{1 + 19(0)} = 200
\end{align*}$$
Since the derivative $\frac{dy}{dt} > 0$ for all $t \ge 0$, the function is strictly increasing.
Thus, the range is $10 \le y < 200$.

$\textbf{(iii)}$
We know $y = \frac{200}{1+19e^{-0.5t}}$, which implies $1+19e^{-0.5t} = \frac{200}{y}$, and $19e^{-0.5t} = \frac{200}{y} - 1 = \frac{200-y}{y}$.
Substitute these into the expression for $\frac{dy}{dt}$:
$$\begin{align*}
\frac{dy}{dt} &= \frac{1900e^{-0.5t}}{(1+19e^{-0.5t})^2} \\
&= \frac{100(19e^{-0.5t})}{(1+19e^{-0.5t})^2} \\
&= \frac{100 \left(\frac{200-y}{y}\right)}{\left(\frac{200}{y}\right)^2} \\
&= \frac{100(200-y)}{y} \times \frac{y^2}{40\,000} \\
&= \frac{100y(200-y)}{40\,000} \\
&= \frac{y(200-y)}{400} \\
&= \frac{y}{400}(200-y)
\end{align*}$$

$\textbf{(iv)}$
The rate of growth $R = \frac{dy}{dt} = \frac{1}{400}(200y - y^2)$.
This is a quadratic function in terms of $y$, which is a concave down parabola.
The maximum rate occurs at the vertex of this parabola.
The roots are $y = 0$ and $y = 200$.
The vertex is exactly halfway between the roots:
$$\begin{align*}
y &= \frac{0 + 200}{2} = 100
\end{align*}$$
Therefore, the population is growing at its fastest rate when $y = 100$.

content.prompt:
$\textbf{(i)}$ Let $y=xu$.
Given that $u$ is a function of $x$, find an expression for $\frac{dy}{dx}$.

$\textbf{(ii)}$ Hence solve the initial value problem $\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{y^2}{2x^2}+\frac{1}{2}$, given $y(1)=2$.
Express your answer with $y$ as the subject.

answer.worked:
$\textbf{(i)}$
Using the product rule:
$$\begin{align*}
y &= xu \\
\frac{dy}{dx} &= u+x\frac{du}{dx}
\end{align*}$$

$\textbf{(ii)}$
Since $y=xu$, $\frac{y^2}{x^2}=u^2$.
$$\begin{align*}
u+x\frac{du}{dx} &= \frac{u^2}{2}+\frac{1}{2} \\
x\frac{du}{dx} &= \frac{u^2-2u+1}{2} \\
x\frac{du}{dx} &= \frac{(u-1)^2}{2} \\
\frac{1}{(u-1)^2}\,du &= \frac{1}{2x}\,dx
\end{align*}$$
Integrate both sides.
$$\begin{align*}
\int (u-1)^{-2}\,du &= \int \frac{1}{2x}\,dx \\
-\frac{1}{u-1} &= \frac{1}{2}\ln x+C \\
\frac{1}{1-u} &= \frac{1}{2}\ln x+C
\end{align*}$$
Use $y(1)=2$. Since $u=\frac{y}{x}$, when $x=1$, $u=2$.
$$\begin{align*}
\frac{1}{1-2} &= \frac{1}{2}\ln 1+C \\
-1 &= C
\end{align*}$$
Hence:
$$\begin{align*}
\frac{1}{1-u} &= \frac{1}{2}\ln x-1 \\
1-u &= \frac{1}{\frac{1}{2}\ln x-1} \\
u &= 1-\frac{1}{\frac{1}{2}\ln x-1} \\
\frac{y}{x} &= 1-\frac{1}{\frac{1}{2}\ln x-1} \\
y &= x-\frac{x}{\frac{1}{2}\ln x-1} \\
y &= x+\frac{2x}{2-\ln x}
\end{align*}$$

content.prompt:
On a certain island, a researcher released $400$ mosquitoes.
The population growth is given by the logistic equation
$$\frac{dP}{dt}=rP\left(1-\frac{P}{16\,000}\right)$$
where $P$ is the population of mosquitoes, $t$ is the number of years after the mosquitoes were released, and $r$ is a constant.
Five years after the mosquitoes were released, the population of mosquitoes was estimated to be $4600$.
It is given that
$$\frac{1}{P(16\,000-P)}=\frac{1}{16\,000}\left(\frac{1}{P}+\frac{1}{16\,000-P}\right).$$

children.label: i
children.prompt: Show by integration that $P=\frac{16\,000}{39e^{-rt}+1}$.

children.label: ii
children.prompt: Hence show that $r=-\frac{1}{5}\ln\left(\frac{19}{299}\right)$.

children.label: iii
children.prompt: When is the population of mosquitoes growing at its fastest rate?

answer.worked:
$\frac{dP}{dt}$ is a quadratic in $P$ with zeros at $0$ and $16\,000$, so it is greatest when $P=8000$.
$$\begin{align*}8000&=\frac{16\,000}{39e^{-rt}+1}\\e^{-rt}&=\frac1{39}\\t&=\frac{\ln39}{r}=\frac{5\ln39}{\ln\frac{299}{19}}\approx6.65\end{align*}$$

children.label: iv
children.prompt: Find the island's carrying capacity for the population of mosquitoes.

children.label: v
children.prompt:
The researcher determines that if the population of mosquitoes exceeds $13\,000$ it will harm the ecosystem of the island.
Spiders are introduced to the island to control the mosquito population, reducing it by $9\%$ every year.
The modified logistic equation for the population growth is
$$\frac{dP}{dt}=rP\left(1-\frac{P}{16\,000}\right)-0.09P.$$
Determine if the researcher will be able to protect the ecosystem from harm.
Justify your answer with the appropriate calculations.

answer.short: No. The population settles at about $13\,388$, which exceeds $13\,000$.
answer.worked:
The population stabilises where $\frac{dP}{dt}=0$ with $P>0$:
$$\begin{align*}r\left(1-\frac P{16\,000}\right)&=0.09\\P&=16\,000\left(1-\frac{0.09}{r}\right)\end{align*}$$
With $r=\frac15\ln\frac{299}{19}\approx0.5513$: $P\approx16\,000(1-0.1633)\approx13\,388$.
Since $13\,388>13\,000$, the researcher will not be able to protect the ecosystem from harm.

entries.description: Solving dy/dx = f(x)

The simplest type of differential equation is \(\frac{dy}{dx}=f(x)\).
To solve these equations, integrate both sides with respect to \(x\).
\[\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx}&=f(x)\\\int\frac{dy}{dx}\,dx&=\int f(x)\,dx\\y&=\int f(x)\,dx\\&=F(x)+C\end{aligned}\]
The general solution of a DE contains constant \(C\) and represents a whole family of curves.
Remember that your solution is an equation; you must have \(y=\cdots\).

entries.description:
y = Ceˣ − x − 1
y′ = Ceˣ − 1

LHS = y′ = Ceˣ − 1

RHS = x + y
= x + (Ceˣ − x − 1)
= Ceˣ − 1

∴ y = Ceˣ − x − 1 satisfies y′ = x + y for all constants C.

entries.description:
An application of differential equations you have seen before is exponential growth and decay.
For exponential change, the rate of change is directly proportional to the current amount.
More quantity means faster change. Less quantity means less change.
Growth constant: k positive for growth; k negative for decay.
If Q = Ae^{kt}, dQ/dt = kAe^{kt} = kQ.
A is labelled “initial quantity”, “t = 0”; k in the exponent is identified by an arrow from the growth-constant annotation.
k gives the growth rate, A is the initial condition.

emphasis: directly proportional to the current amount
More quantity means faster change. Less quantity means less change.

entries.description:
In realistic models of growth and decay, the change is proportional to the difference of the current value to some constant value, P.
Larger difference means faster change. Smaller difference means slower change.
If Q = P + Ae^{kt}, dQ/dt = kAe^{kt}
= k(P + Ae^{kt} − P)
= k(Q − P).
An underbrace beneath P + A labels it “initial quantity”, “t = 0”.
The left graph is labelled k < 0, A > 0. The right graph is labelled k < 0, A < 0.
When k < 0 (decreasing growth), the quantity Q approaches a limiting value P as t → ∞.
This limiting value P can represent:
• ambient temperature; hot objects cool towards room temperature.
• carrying capacity; populations stabilise at the maximum an environment can support.
P is a horizontal isocline of the slope field, representing the constant asymptotic solution.

emphasis: Larger difference means faster change. Smaller difference means slower change.

entries.description:
dP/dt = kP(1 − P/C)

The logistic equation models growth that is limited by a carrying capacity C.
kP represents exponential growth, and (1 − P/C) represents the constraints of the environment.
When P = C, (1 − P/C) = 0 and growth stops.

Logistic growth in a population begins slowly as few individuals reproduce, accelerates as the population grows, then slows as it approaches the environment's carrying capacity.

[Paired graphs]

The logistic equation has horizontal isoclines representing constant asymptotic solutions at P = 0 and P = C. All solution curves will tend to converge towards P = C.
Usually, the scenario limits the domain and range to t ≥ 0 and P > 0.

Alternate notation:
P′ = kP(C − P): C is expanded into the brackets; k is different to the original.

entries.description:
The general form of a logistic differential equation dP/dt = kP(1 − P/C) is

P = C/(1 + Ae^(−kt)) where A = (C − P₀)/P₀.

Note that you cannot memorise this. The questions will require you to solve the DE.
To solve the DE, you will be given a partial fraction decomposition and follow these steps:

1. Invert both sides of the DE to get dt/dP.
2. Match the integrand to the given partial fractions.
3. Integrate both sides; use D as the constant of integration.
4. Combine ln a − ln b = ln(a/b) and isolate.
5. Exponentiate and write ±e^(c/k) as a single arbitrary constant A.
6. Substitute the initial condition to find A.
7. Rearrange to make P the subject.
8. Divide through by e^(kt) to reach the general form P = C/(1 + Be^(−kt)).

We will first practice the purely algebraic case where there is no context.

entries.description:
A colony of rabbits has carrying capacity 1200 and satisfies
\[\frac{dP}{dt}=kP\left(1-\frac{P}{1200}\right),\qquad P(0)=200,\quad P(2)=400,\]
where k is an unknown constant and t is in years.
Use \(\frac{1200}{P(1200-P)}=\frac1P+\frac1{1200-P}\).
Find P(t) and hence P(5).
entries.presentation: Black question text; centred differential equation and initial conditions. Unbordered working space below. The supplied decomposition establishes the separation-of-variables and partial-fractions method.

entries.description:
Supplied blue working:
\[\frac{dt}{dP}=\frac1k\left(\frac1P+\frac1{1200-P}\right)\Rightarrow\frac{P}{1200-P}=Ae^{kt}.\]
\[P(0)=200:\quad\frac{200}{1000}=A\Rightarrow A=\frac15,\text{ so }P=\frac{1200}{1+5e^{-kt}}.\]
Find k using P(2)=400:
\[400=\frac{1200}{1+5e^{-2k}}\Rightarrow1+5e^{-2k}=3\Rightarrow e^{-2k}=0.4.\]
\[k=-\frac12\ln0.4=\frac12\ln2.5\approx0.4581.\]
\[P(5)=\frac{1200}{1+5e^{-5k}},\text{ where }e^{-5k}=(0.4)^{2.5}\approx0.1012.\]
\[P(5)=\frac{1200}{1.5060}\approx797.\]

entries.description: Solve the differential equation to find the formula for the height of the tree.

Separate variables:
[1/(Q(45 − Q))] dQ = 0.03 dt
Using partial fractions from (a):
(1/45)(1/Q + 1/(45 − Q)) dQ = 0.03 dt
Integrate both sides:
(1/45)(ln|Q| − ln|45 − Q|) = 0.03t + C
ln|Q/(45 − Q)| = 1.35t + C
Q/(45 − Q) = Ae^(1.35t)
Sub initial condition Q = 0.3 when t = 0:
0.3/44.7 = A → A = 1/149
So: Q/(45 − Q) = (1/149)e^(1.35t)
149Q = (45 − Q)e^(1.35t)
149Q + Qe^(1.35t) = 45e^(1.35t)
Q(149 + e^(1.35t)) = 45e^(1.35t)
Q = 45e^(1.35t)/(149 + e^(1.35t))
Divide numerator and denominator by e^(1.35t):
Q = 45/(1 + 149e^(−1.35t))

entries.description:
The population of kangaroos, P (in thousands), in bushland satisfies
\[\frac{dP}{dt}=0.1P\left(1-\frac{P}{C}\right)\]
where t is the number of years after 2000 and C is the carrying capacity.

In 2000 there were 15 000 kangaroos. By 2020 there were 60 000 kangaroos.

Use the fact that \(\frac{C}{P(C-P)}=\frac{1}{P}+\frac{1}{C-P}\) to show the carrying capacity is approx. 113 000.

Follow these steps:
entries.presentation: Differential equation centred on its own line. Emphasise “in thousands”. Preserve the supplied partial-fraction identity and the two numbered steps in order. Large blank working region below the steps.

entries.description: 1. Show that the general solution is \(\frac{P}{C-P}=Ae^{t/10}\).
entries.expectedAnswer: \(\frac{P}{C-P}=Ae^{t/10}\), supplied as the result to establish.

entries.description: 2. Use the two data points to solve simultaneously for C.
entries.expectedAnswer: Carrying capacity approximately 113 000 kangaroos, as supplied in the question.

entries.description:
Kosciusko National Park has feral horses called brumbies.
Brumbies are considered pests as they damage the soil and waterways.
Their natural population P satisfies dP/dt = 0.5P(1 − P/20 000), with t in years.
To control it, a culling programme aims to remove 10% of the population each year, giving
 dP/dt = 0.5P(1 − P/20 000) − 0.1P
Populations above 15 000 damage the habitat.
Determine whether the culling programme would be effective in preventing this damage.
entries.presentation: Black question text; natural-population equation inline and culling-model equation centred on a separate line. Unruled working space below. No parts, diagrams or tables.

entries.description: Supplied blue worked answer, separate from the student prompt.
entries.expectedAnswer:
Find the non-zero equilibrium (where dP/dt = 0):
P[0.5(1 − P/20 000) − 0.1] = 0
For P ≠ 0:
0.5(1 − P/20 000) = 0.1
1 − P/20 000 = 0.2
P = 16 000
The population settles at 16 000.
Since 16 000 > 15 000, the culling programme is not ambitious enough to prevent damage to the habitat.

entries.description:
An application of differential equations you have seen before is exponential growth and decay.
For exponential change, the rate of change is directly proportional to the current amount.
More quantity means faster change. Less quantity means less change.
Growth constant: k positive for growth; k negative for decay.
If Q = Ae^{kt}, dQ/dt = kAe^{kt} = kQ.
A is labelled “initial quantity”, “t = 0”; k in the exponent is identified by an arrow from the growth-constant annotation.
k gives the growth rate, A is the initial condition.
entries.mappingNote: The same independently inventoried source teaching passage continues in this separately authored native wrapper. Source text and original inventory entry retained; current independent content review covers this exact wrapper.

entries.description:
In realistic models of growth and decay, the change is proportional to the difference of the current value to some constant value, P.
Larger difference means faster change. Smaller difference means slower change.
If Q = P + Ae^{kt}, dQ/dt = kAe^{kt}
= k(P + Ae^{kt} − P)
= k(Q − P).
An underbrace beneath P + A labels it “initial quantity”, “t = 0”.
The left graph is labelled k < 0, A > 0. The right graph is labelled k < 0, A < 0.
When k < 0 (decreasing growth), the quantity Q approaches a limiting value P as t → ∞.
This limiting value P can represent:
• ambient temperature; hot objects cool towards room temperature.
• carrying capacity; populations stabilise at the maximum an environment can support.
P is a horizontal isocline of the slope field, representing the constant asymptotic solution.

entries.description:
dP/dt = kP(1 − P/C)

The logistic equation models growth that is limited by a carrying capacity C.
kP represents exponential growth, and (1 − P/C) represents the constraints of the environment.
When P = C, (1 − P/C) = 0 and growth stops.

Logistic growth in a population begins slowly as few individuals reproduce, accelerates as the population grows, then slows as it approaches the environment's carrying capacity.

[Paired graphs]

The logistic equation has horizontal isoclines representing constant asymptotic solutions at P = 0 and P = C. All solution curves will tend to converge towards P = C.
Usually, the scenario limits the domain and range to t ≥ 0 and P > 0.

Alternate notation:
P′ = kP(C − P): C is expanded into the brackets; k is different to the original.
